query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Ultrafine-grained (UFG) microstructure enhances the formation and long-term stability of a protective Cr-rich passive film even under thermal fluctuations and moderate irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless steel with coarse grains and standard Cr content.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion or friction stir processing) to refine the grain structure while ensuring processing parameters that minimize grain growth during later high-temperature service.
generation.conditions: Exposure to chloride-containing aqueous solutions or simulated nuclear reactor water/steam environments at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures, including conditions with intermittent irradiation or thermal aging.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary density accelerates Cr transport and results in a uniform and thicker Cr-rich oxide film; attention is given to a controlled grain size distribution that remains stable under service conditions.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced grain boundary diffusion of Cr in the UFG steel promotes rapid formation of a homogeneous, adherent Cr-rich passive layer. This film is more stable under thermal fluctuations and moderate irradiation because the refined microstructure retains its grain size distribution and resists grain growth.
generation.predicted_outcome: UFG steels will display a significantly thicker and more uniform Cr-rich passive film, lower corrosion current density, and sustained passivation performance during long-term cyclic thermal and low-level irradiation exposures compared to coarse-grained steels.
generation.baseline: Standard coarse-grained stainless steel with slower Cr diffusion and a thinner, less uniform passive film.
generation.boundary: Valid for steels with adequate Cr content under moderate corrosive environments and service temperatures; may not hold under extreme high temperatures or highly aggressive irradiative environments that induce rapid microstructural degradation.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains in precisely quantifying the trade-off between accelerated diffusion and potential grain coarsening during extended high-temperature service, and the impact of concurrent irradiation on grain stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical stainless steel samples from the same alloy; one set is processed to have an ultrafine-grained (UFG) structure via SPD with controlled parameters, and the other retains a coarse-grained structure. Both sets are subjected to prolonged exposure in simulated corrosive environments that mimic reactor water/steam conditions, including thermal cycling and low-dose irradiation.
measurements: Electrochemical polarization tests to measure corrosion current density and potential
XPS/TEM/EBSD analysis to evaluate passive film composition, thickness, and grain size stability over time
Long-term corrosion rate and pit density assessments under thermal cycling conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the UFG steel does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in passive film thickness, uniformity, and lower corrosion current density or if its microstructural refinement is lost during exposure, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As a well-known high-entropy alloys (HEA), equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, also known as Cantor alloy, has been increasingly investigated in recent years, with a focus on enhanced fracture toughness and ductility at cryogenic temperatures []. HEAs could become future materials for structural applications due to these superior properties. However, compared with the mechanical properties, the corrosion properties, which are also important for structural applications, have not been investigated to the same extent. The majority of HEAs, as represented by Cantor alloy, have a higher amount of Cr and Ni compared to commercial stainless steels (SS) such as AISI304, so that they are expected to exhibit high corrosion resistance, and they have been demonstrated to possess high passivating capability in neutral solutions [,,,,,]. However, it seems that the corrosion resistance of HEAs is not necessarily as high as expected given the large Cr and Ni content [,,], and in particular the pitting corrosion resistance in chloride-containing environments is inferior to AISI304 [,,]. Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed. One is the selective dissolution of Fe and oxidation of Cr due to the high chemical reactivity of the UFG structure [,], and the second is fast diffusi

The present results for CoCrFeMnNi alloys on the stable passivation composition against UFG formation (or less sensitive composition to grain size than Fe–Cr alloys) can be explained by considering some high-entropy effects, which are among the four core effects of HEAs. The high-entropy effect of HEAs decreases the possibility of elemental segregation or local enrichment of specific elements and favors the formation of a uniform distribution of component elements. Therefore, the selective dissolution of specific elements, which leads to local enrichment of the other remaining elements, increases the mixing enthalpy and may destabilize the fcc phase. Thus, selective dissolution could be suppressed during anodic dissolution. Luo et al. conducted an in situ element-resolved corrosion analysis using online ICP-MS analysis and concluded that no obvious selective dissolution of Mn, Co, Ni and Fe occurred during surface passivation of the equiatomic HEA in 0.1 M H2SO4 []. The second reason for the small influence of grain size on the corrosion behavior of CrCoFeMnNi alloys compared with Fe–Cr alloys is related to diffusion. The corrosion behavior of UFG CoCrFeMnNi alloys processed by HPT with Cr contents ranging from 0 to 20 at.% was investigated in 3.5% NaCl and 0.5 M H2SO4 solutions and compared to homogenized coarse-grained (CG) counterpart materials. Several conclusions were obtained, as follows. The polarization curves in 1 M H2SO4 solution showed the active–passive, passive and transpassive behavior typical of binary Fe–Cr alloys. An increase in Cr content decreased the potential of the active–passive transition, and thus increased the ability to passivate. Cr was the dominant element providing the passivation ability. The polarization curves in 1 M H2SO4 solution showed little difference between the coarse-grained state after homogenization and the nanocrystalline structure after HPT. The impact of nanocrystalline structure on corrosion was negligibly small. Similarly, corrosion resistance to pitting in 3.5% NaCl solution was also little affected by the formation of the nanocrystalline structure, and this is in striking contrast to the high corrosion resistance of nanocrystalline or ultrafine-grained stainless steels processed by SPD reported elsewhere.
